title: Safe choices offline and online
subject: PSHE
label: Public edition
objective_verbatim: Recognise safe and unsafe situations, offline and online.
assessment_verbatim: F: scenario sorting.  S: 'my trusted network' + safe/unsafe task (Dec).

Read-only planning source. Workbook not redistributed.

external_sources.title: NHS Live Well
external_sources.supports: General healthy living includes food, movement and sleep; no individual medical prescription is made.

external_sources.title: NHS Physical activity for children and young people
external_sources.supports: Movement should suit the young person and activity; break up sitting and use appropriate safety measures.

external_sources.title: PSHE Association Handling complex issues safely
external_sources.supports: Ground rules, fictional scenarios, an option to pass and appropriate safeguarding responses.

external_sources.title: CEOP Education Reporting and blocking
external_sources.supports: Ask a trusted adult for help with pressure online; use the platform reporting and blocking tools with support. Reporting does not guarantee removal.

external_sources.title: CEOP Education Staying private online
external_sources.supports: Privacy controls can limit who sees information. They do not prove the identity or intentions of a sender.

evidence.description: Individual scenario judgement with clue, reason, safer next step and response after feedback.

routes.Supported: Two cases read aloud; point, say or draw and give a reason.
routes.Independent: Six cases; explain one on the Evidence Sheet.
routes.Aspire: Six cases; identify a missing fact that could change a judgement.

vocab.definition: For you or people you choose.
An adult you can ask for help.

cases.text: A message offers a prize. It asks for your password.
cases.next_step: Do not reply or open links. Ask a trusted adult.
cases.staff_note: A lock or gift icon is not proof that a message is genuine.

cases.text: A friend wants to post a photo of you. You have said no.
cases.clue: Your permission has not been given.
cases.next_step: Ask them not to share it. Get adult help if needed.
cases.staff_note: Do not blame the person in the photo. If already shared, seek adult help with reporting.

cases.text: The teacher gives the class a checked page for a task. You use that page.
cases.clue: The teacher has checked that page for the task.
cases.next_step: Stay on the set task and ask if something new appears.
cases.staff_note: Checking one page does not guarantee every link or pop-up is safe.

cases.text: A friend dares you to climb a locked gate.
cases.clue: The gate is locked and the dare adds pressure.
cases.next_step: Keep clear. Say no or move away and tell an adult.
cases.staff_note: Refusal can be quiet or supported; no role-play of the unsafe action.

cases.text: A new pop-up asks you to click. It appears on a class page.
cases.clue: We do not know what the new pop-up is.
cases.next_step: Pause. Do not click. Ask the teacher.
cases.staff_note: The site context alone does not establish that the new content is safe.

cases.text: You are worried. A trusted staff member offers to listen in the agreed space.
cases.clue: Help is offered through the school support route.
cases.next_step: Say what help you need. You can use the private-help card.
cases.staff_note: Known people can act unsafely too. Judge behaviour, not appearance. Adults cannot promise secrecy.

What clue helps us choose a safer step?
I can spot a clue offline or online. I can explain why a choice may be unsafe. I can choose a safer step and ask for help.
GROW-PSHE-W2-E1: individual scenario choice, clue, reason and safer next step, with a short check after feedback. Accept pointing, speech, drawing or writing; scribe only the learner’s own response.

Prepare the deck, one Evidence Sheet and Vocabulary Mat per learner, and one set of Support Cards. The Support Cards contain the six cases, sort labels, a picture prompt and a private-help card. Have pens and a timer ready. No food tasting, risky action, live messages, log-ins or web searches are required.

Identify the staff member and agreed place for private help before teaching. Read the Staff Answers and local safeguarding route. Check the room route is clear. Offer a quiet seat and a supported movement break. Keep the vocabulary mat in view.

Week 2 runs Monday 9 to Friday 13 November. The owner supplied a week range, not a lesson day or clock time. Enter the actual teaching date above. The later Week 5 calendar correction is outside this piece.
Open title and big question before timing.
Private check-in. Choose quiet start, water, seated stretch or adult help. Read the right-to-pass rule.
Use the picture prompt. Point to one clue and hear a possible next step.
Read the exact objective and the three I can checks.
Think aloud through the model. Separate the clue from a guess.
Read the hinge. Pupils point, say or write A, B or C and a reason.
Sort fictional cases. Use the route that fits current access needs.
Complete the individual Evidence Sheet. Adult records actual support.
Check evidence, put cards away and choose one next step.
Hear a short response to the exit questions.
Keep the vocabulary mat available throughout.

C. A password is private. Pause and ask a trusted adult without replying or opening links. A shares private details; B puts someone else at risk. If a response misses the risk, return to the visible clue, model the safer step and use one new case before individual capture. A correct letter without a reason is not enough to check understanding.

Supported: begin with two cases read aloud. Point to a sort label and clue; tell or draw one next step. Independent: sort all six, then explain one choice on the Evidence Sheet. Aspire: sort all six and show how one missing fact could change a judgement. The adult may read or scribe without supplying the reason.

There is no forced pair work, personal disclosure, cold calling or public performance. Allow processing time, a quiet adult response and an option to pass. After a pass, offer an alternative fictional case privately; do not infer attainment from silence.

Keep all examples fictional. Do not ask pupils to describe home routines, health conditions, private messages or past harm. Use respectful language about food, bodies, disability and family circumstances. A behaviour can be unsafe even when the person is familiar. Avoid judging safety from appearance.

Offer the phrase “Can I speak to you in private?” If a concern is raised, listen calmly, avoid investigating in class and follow the setting’s safeguarding procedure. Never promise secrecy. Explain that a relevant adult may need to help. Keep safeguarding records separate from the lesson evidence. If a learner is not heard, help them reach another trusted adult.

Check the clue, judgement, reason and next step against the Staff Answers. Accept a different judgement where the learner gives a valid reason and identifies what must be checked. “Safer” means reduced risk, not a guarantee. Record the case ID, actual words/actions, response mode, support and feedback. A copied model or blank form is not completed evidence.

Use the established marking codes VF, WS, I, NS, +, //, ?, R and E as appropriate. Retain the learner’s response after feedback. R records voice, audience, next step and the learner’s own response; it is not an assumed success judgement.

Space: quiet, non-personal ways to respond. Voice: the learner chooses the case and explains their own view. Audience: the teaching adult hears or reads the response and replies. Influence: record the learner’s requested support or next practice step and how the next task changes.

Possible communication evidence: explain a clue, listen to another reason, ask for clarification, and write or dictate a safer next step. The receiving teacher can select authentic responses for their own portfolio requirements; this lesson assigns no communication criterion numbers.

GROW-PSHE-W2-E1 · Safe choices offline and online
Use a made-up case. Point, say, draw or write. An adult can write your own words.
If I need help, I can say: Can I speak to you in private?
After the adult’s feedback, I changed or checked
One clue online that would make me pause is
Response: spoken / pointed / drawn / written / adult scribe
Check: clue / reason / next step / response after feedback. Mark what was seen and what still needs practice. Do not record a private safeguarding account here.
These are model responses for fictional cases. They are not observations of a learner. Allow a different defensible answer when the reason and next step fit the facts.
Risk. It asks for a password.
Do not reply or open links. Ask a trusted adult.
Risk. Your permission has not been given.
Ask them not to share it. Get adult help if needed.
Safer. The teacher has checked that page for the task.
Stay on the set task and ask if something new appears.
Risk. The gate is locked and the dare adds pressure.
Keep clear. Say no or move away and tell an adult.
Need more information. We do not know what the new pop-up is.
Pause. Do not click. Ask the teacher.
Safer. Help is offered through the school support route.
Say what help you need. You can use the private-help card.
Jo sees a message about a free prize. It asks Jo to share a password. Clue: it asks for private details. Jo pauses and does not reply. Jo shows a trusted adult. They check the next step together.
C. A password is private. Pause and ask a trusted adult without replying or opening links. A shares private details; B puts someone else at risk.
Ask: What is the clue? What could happen? What can the person do next? Give thinking time and offer a quiet response. Record an actual reason, not just a correct letter or a completed sort.
Case A: A lock or gift icon is not proof that a message is genuine.
Case B: Do not blame the person in the photo. If already shared, seek adult help with reporting.
Case C: Checking one page does not guarantee every link or pop-up is safe.
Case D: Refusal can be quiet or supported; no role-play of the unsafe action.
Case E: The site context alone does not establish that the new content is safe.
Case F: Known people can act unsafely too. Judge behaviour, not appearance. Adults cannot promise secrecy.

A familiar person, a colourful icon or a checked space does not make every later action safe. “Need more information” is useful when a missing fact matters; it is not a reason to try the risky action. “Safer” recognises reduced risk without claiming certainty.

Keep passwords private. Never ask pupils to show actual messages or account details. If something has already gone wrong, the learner still deserves help. Use adult support with the platform’s reporting/blocking tools where relevant; reporting cannot guarantee removal.

If the clue is vague, point to the case and ask which words helped. If the step increases risk, re-model a pause and an adult check. If a learner is ready, ask what extra fact would change the answer. Preserve the learner’s own revised response, the adult’s support and the next practice need.

Identify the real school support route before the lesson. Listen to concerns, do not investigate in class and never promise secrecy. Follow local safeguarding procedures and keep those records separate. Use fictional alternatives and a right to pass. See the planner and FACTS_LEDGER.md for sources.
